ego.name: Konrad Zuse
ego.summary: Konrad Zuse was a German civil engineer, inventor, and entrepreneur who developed the Z1, Z3, and Z4 computing machines and designed the Plankalkül programming language. He founded Zuse KG after World War II.

connections.relationship_description: Konrad Zuse's mother, Maria Zuse raised him with Emil Zuse in Berlin, Braunsberg, and Hoyerswerda. The family home later gave him space for the Z1 workshop.
connections.notes: The family apartment in Berlin later housed Zuse's workshop for the Z1.

connections.relationship_description: Konrad Zuse's father, Emil Zuse worked as a postal official. He returned from retirement to help finance his son's early computer development.
connections.notes: Zuse built the Z1 in his parents' Berlin apartment.

connections.relationship_description: Gisela Brandes was Konrad Zuse's wife and the mother of their five children. She shared the practical demands of family life during the years of Zuse KG.
connections.notes: Their marriage lasted until Konrad Zuse's death in 1995.

connections.relationship_description: Horst Zuse was Konrad Zuse's eldest son and became a computer scientist who later reconstructed the Z3 and published books about his father.
connections.notes: Born in 1945, Horst Zuse helped preserve and interpret his father's computing legacy.

connections.relationship_description: Helmut Schreyer met Zuse through the AV Motiv student association in 1937. He became a friend and collaborator in Zuse's early computer work, including the Z3.
connections.notes: In 1938, they demonstrated a vacuum-tube switching circuit and discussed building an electronic computer; Schreyer collaborated on the Z3 presented in 1941.

connections.relationship_description: Eduard Stiefel visited Zuse in the Allgäu in 1949 to inspect the Z4, then arranged its rental for use at ETH Zurich.
connections.notes: The Z4 rental supplied crucial funds that enabled Zuse to found Zuse KG in 1949.

connections.relationship_description: Monika Zuse was one of Konrad Zuse and Gisela Brandes's five children.
Ernst Zuse was one of Konrad Zuse and Gisela Brandes's five children.
Hannelore Zuse was one of Konrad Zuse and Gisela Brandes's five children.
Peter Zuse was one of Konrad Zuse and Gisela Brandes's five children.
Wilfried de Beauclair met Zuse in Berlin in 1942 and saw the Z3. He later supported work on the Z4 with punched-tape equipment from Darmstadt.
connections.notes: Their technical cooperation developed into a friendship.

connections.relationship_description: Herbert Wagner helped secure Zuse's classification as indispensable for wartime work at Henschel. The intervention kept Zuse out of military deployment.
connections.notes: This intervention kept Zuse from military deployment and enabled his work on specialized computing devices for the Hs 293 project.

connections.relationship_description: Günther Bock helped finance development of the Z3 after Zuse demonstrated the Z2 in 1940. He acted through the German Aeronautical Research Institute.
connections.notes: Bock later negotiated institutional cooperation with Zuse during his directorship of the German Aeronautical Research Institute.

connections.relationship_description: Zuse's team briefly traveled with Wernher von Braun's evacuation group near the end of World War II. The association arose during the flight from Berlin with the Z4.
connections.notes: Their direct association was brief and arose from the wartime evacuation.

connections.relationship_description: Zuse presented his applied logic and ideas related to Plankalkül in Wilhelm Britzelmayr's logic colloquia at Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich during the winter semester of 1948–49.
connections.notes: The colloquia gave Zuse an early postwar forum for his programming-language ideas.

connections.relationship_description: Konrad Zuse and Heinz Billing took part in a 1947 colloquium with British computing specialists, where German researchers discussed binary numbers and data storage.
connections.notes: The meeting linked Zuse to other early postwar German computer pioneers and international specialists.

connections.relationship_description: Konrad Zuse and Alwin Walther were among the German computer researchers who participated in a 1947 exchange with British scientists and computing specialists.
connections.notes: Walther's Darmstadt institute also indirectly assisted Zuse's Z4 work through Wilfried de Beauclair and its punched-tape equipment.

category_summaries.summary: Zuse's parents gave his first computer work a practical base. Their Berlin apartment housed the Z1 workshop, and Emil Zuse returned from retirement to help fund development. Gisela Brandes and their children shared the disruptions of the 1945 flight and the demands of running Zuse KG. Their eldest son, Horst, later documented and reconstructed parts of his father's technical work.

Zuse relied on collaborators who could help turn designs into working machines. Helmut Schreyer worked with him on early computing projects and the Z3. Wilfried de Beauclair supplied practical support for the Z4. Eduard Stiefel arranged the Z4 rental to ETH Zurich in 1949, bringing the funds that supported Zuse KG.

Wartime employers and funders gave Zuse access to resources for computer development. Herbert Wagner secured Zuse's protected work position at Henschel. Günther Bock helped obtain funding for the Z3 through the German Aeronautical Research Institute. During the evacuation from Berlin, Zuse's team briefly traveled with Wernher von Braun's group while carrying the Z4 toward Bavaria.

Academic contacts brought Zuse's independent engineering work into postwar discussions of logic and computing. Wilhelm Britzelmayr's Munich colloquium gave Zuse a forum for ideas related to Plankalkül in 1948 and 1949. Contacts with Heinz Billing and Alwin Walther connected him with other German researchers working on electronic and numerical computing.
